title: Your first repository and commit
objective: By the end of this lesson you can turn any folder into a repository, and you understand the staging area well enough to commit deliberately rather than committing everything by reflex.

blocks.text: Git tracks a folder once you tell it to. From that moment the folder has a hidden .git directory holding the entire history, and everything you do happens locally — no account, no server, no network.

blocks.caption: Starting a repository
lines: git init                 # this folder now has a history

blocks.title: The .git directory is the repository
blocks.text: Delete it and you delete every commit, every branch, and the entire history — the files in the folder stay, but their past is gone. Copy it and you have copied the project. Never edit anything inside it by hand.
Three places a file can be

rows: The files as they are on disk right now
The changes you have chosen for the next commit

blocks.text: The staging area is the part newcomers find strange and experienced people find indispensable. It exists so a commit can be a deliberate selection rather than everything you happen to have touched. You changed three things; two of them belong together and one does not; stage the two, commit them, then handle the third separately.

blocks.caption: The everyday loop
lines: git status                    # untracked: Git can see it but is not tracking it
git add .                     # stage every change below this directory
git commit -m "Message that says why, not what"

blocks.title: git add . is convenient and worth a second of care
blocks.text: It stages everything, including files you did not mean to include — a temporary dump, a local config, a key. Run git status first and read the list. That one habit prevents most accidental commits, and it is the same look-then-act rule that applies to deleting files.
Writing a message that will still be useful

The diff already shows what changed. The message exists to record why, for the person reading it in six months, who is usually you. A good message is one line, in the imperative, describing the effect.

rows: States the effect, not the activity
Fix timezone shift on the report export
Move rate limiting into the middleware
A history is read by people

blocks.title: Why the message matters more than it looks
blocks.text: Every investigation into a change — a regression, an outage, an audit — starts by reading messages to find the commit worth opening. A history of 'update' and 'fix' forces you to open all of them.

blocks.title: Make a repository with three commits
steps: Run: echo 'line one' > notes.txt && git status
Run: git add notes.txt && git commit -m "Start the notes file"
Run: echo 'line two' >> notes.txt && echo 'draft' > scratch.tmp
Run: git status                     (two changes: one you want, one you do not)
Run: git add notes.txt && git commit -m "Add the second note"
Run: git log --oneline              (your history so far)
blocks.expected: Two commits, and scratch.tmp still sitting untracked — which is exactly the point of staging: you chose what entered the history instead of sweeping in everything present.

cheatsheet: git init turns the current folder into a repository
.git holds the entire history — deleting it deletes the past
Working directory → staging area (git add) → repository (git commit)
Staging exists so a commit is a deliberate selection, not a sweep
git status before git add . — read what you are about to include
git commit -m "..." records the staged changes with a message
Write the message in the imperative and say why, not what
git log --oneline reads the history back

checkpoint.prompt: What is the staging area for?

choices.B: Choosing exactly which changes go into the next commit, instead of committing everything you touched
choices.C: A queue of files waiting to upload to a server
choices.D: A cache that makes Git faster

checkpoint.explanation: It separates 'I changed this' from 'this belongs in this commit', which is what lets a history be made of coherent, single-purpose commits.

checkpoint.prompt: You delete the .git directory from a project folder. What happens?

choices.A: Nothing — it is a cache and Git rebuilds it
choices.B: The files remain but every commit, branch, and piece of history is gone
choices.D: The project reverts to its first commit

checkpoint.explanation: .git is the repository itself. Without it the folder is just files with no past — and no way to recover one locally.

checkpoint.prompt: Which commit message is most useful six months later?
checkpoint.explanation: It states the effect of the change. The diff already shows what lines moved; the message is there to say why, so the right commit can be found without opening every one.

checkpoint.prompt: Why run git status before git add . ?

choices.B: It shows exactly what is about to be included, so a temporary file, local config, or key does not get swept into the commit
choices.D: It stages the files for you

checkpoint.explanation: Look before you act. Once a file is committed, removing it later does not remove it from the history.
